question: Should the Hijri month, including Ramadan and Eid, begin by moon sighting or by astronomical calculations?
answer:
Today, insha'Allah ta'ala, we will summarize the positions of the modern councils and the other opinions in this regard, and discuss why certain ulama hold positions that are pro-calculations and others hold positions that are anti-calculations.

Before I begin the fiqh issue, I would like to take a step back and ask ourselves: why is it that this particular issue, out of all of the areas of difference of opinion, generates the type of controversy, or the type of quick anger, or the type of heated debate, or frankly even the emotionalism, that other topics do not generate? I find this interesting because we all know that there are so many gray areas of fiqh. We all know that the different scholars have given different positions about so many areas of Islamic law. And these areas don't generate the type of antagonism or the type of anger or animosity that this one issue does.

In fact, subhanAllah, I'm going to give you one example that comes to my mind right now: sometimes there's even a hadith that might seem to suggest that the person who doesn't follow this position is going to go to Jahannam. For example, there's a hadith that our Prophet ﷺ saw a lady wearing bangles, wearing jewelry, and he said, "Do you give zakat on the gold that you have?" And she said no. And so the Prophet ﷺ said, "Then you are wearing bracelets from Jahannam." This is an authentic hadith, by the way.

Now, I'm just giving an example. In fact, the majority of the madhhabs, three of the four madhhabs, said that zakat is not due on a woman's jewelry. Can you believe that? And they found ways to understand this hadith; they said this hadith means this, it means that. So three of the four madhhabs said that a woman does not give zakat on her gold jewelry. Only the Hanafi madhhab said that she gives zakat on jewelry.

Now, what I find interesting: you don't find people going around asking, "Do you pay zakat? If not, a'udhu billah, you're going to Jahannam." We understand that both schools, or both opinions, looked at the goals of the Shari'ah. They had ways of understanding the tradition. The majority of ulama, of the ummah actually, in this particular case understood these hadith in a way that goes against what the average reader would derive from them. The point is not which one is right or wrong. The point is that we don't find any emotionalism. We understand that our scholars differ.

The same goes for so many other issues that we find in our times: about the arkan of salah, about the timings of salah, the Asr prayer between the Hanafi madhhab versus the other three madhhabs. The Hanbalis say that Salat al-Jumu'ah can be prayed before Salat al-Dhuhr, so many masajid in North America opt into the Hanbali madhhab, because it allows them to pray even before the zawal time, because in the Hanbali madhhab the timing of Dhuhr is not the same as Jumu'ah, for example. And we don't find the community splitting up, or so much anger.

So we need to ask ourselves, before I even talk about the fiqh: why so much division? Why so much sparking of anger? It's a difficult question to answer, because this is a psychological issue, not a fiqh one: why there is so much ikhtilaf and whatnot. I have an opinion, I have a theory. It could be right, could be wrong.

The theory is as follows: what we are seeing now is that there are so many radical reformations going on, radical reinterpretations, and this issue has been sucked up and made into one of those radical reformations. To be more explicit here: what we are seeing in our current situation is that there are certain groups of people, certain Muslims, who wish to genuinely protect the Qur'an and Sunnah and follow the Qur'an and Sunnah. They're interested in classical Islamic law. They want to maintain their Islamic identity as passed down for 14 centuries. Alhamdulillah, I consider myself to be amongst that group.

On the flip side, we have a group of people who identify as Muslims, but by and large they're not that concerned about the sanctity of our sacred texts. They're not concerned about the tradition, and they're willing to entirely discard the mainstream interpretations of Islamic law and invent, frankly, a completely new system, a completely new law. And the examples are well known: for example, the morality of genders in terms of sexuality — the LGBT issue, for example, they want to reinterpret completely; or the claim that a Muslim lady can marry outside of the faith, which is totally unprecedented in classical Islamic law; or that a mixed congregation can have the khutbah given by a female imam and be led by a female imam. These are examples of that strand.

Clearly it's a very contentious issue, and people are legitimately concerned that we're going to continue to change the Shari'ah or water down the Shari'ah. It's a legitimate fear. So what happens is that when some of our brothers or sisters see any opinion that they've never heard of before, understandably there is a reaction that is a protective one. And it's a positive feeling, that you want to protect the Shari'ah, and there's a reaction that, hey, we're not going to go down that avenue, we're going to shut the door to any change.

But you see, our Shari'ah does not ask us to react to one emotional tendency with another one. No doubt, radical reinterpretation is haram. No doubt, coming up with a completely new set of laws of Shari'ah or whatnot cannot be something that is valid in our Shari'ah. But the question arises: is every single change opening the door to a discarding of the Shari'ah? Obviously not. And therefore, who gets to decide? It is our respected ulama, and their track records and their reputation speak for themselves. It is our ulama who will decide, based upon the science known as usul al-fiqh.

And of course, this topic that we are doing is general awareness. I don't expect anybody to listen to a lecture or two and then decide for himself or herself which one they're going to follow. This is general awareness. The example that I give: I'm not a medical doctor. If I were to go to a medical doctor and something is diagnosed in me — Allah protect all of us — the doctor would explain to me and contextualize for me and tell me, hey, this is happening, and this is the result, and this is the treatment. Now, I'm not a doctor; I'm not qualified to challenge what the doctor is saying. But there's a reason why the doctor is going to explain it to me: so that I begin to understand.

Similarly, this lecture that I'm giving, this answer that I'm giving, is meant to explain. It is meant to educate. It is meant to increase awareness. It is not meant to substitute for the actual training and study which the ulama or the students of knowledge do for many, many years.

So we have to be willing to engage in dialogue and listen to the other side. And I ask in this regard that both of these sides respect the other side and understand that both of them wish to follow the Sunnah. It is an egregious, a very dangerous, a very evil accusation when you call another Muslim and say, "You don't want to follow the Sunnah." It's a very dangerous and a very bitter accusation that is simply not true. Both sides want to follow the Sunnah, insha'Allah ta'ala, in this regard, as this lecture will explain. But the point is: how does one interpret the Sunnah? How does one interpret the goals of the Shari'ah?

I've given in other lectures the example of the Asr prayer of Banu Qurayzah, when the Prophet made a statement: "Do not pray Asr until you get to Banu Qurayzah." And the Sahabah themselves were divided. Should we literally follow "do not pray Asr", make Asr qada and then pray after Salat al-Maghrib, which is what one group did? Or, the other group said, well, okay, the Prophet said that and he meant this, but there are certain extenuating circumstances. There are certain contexts: when he gave that, he didn't know that we would be in this particular situation. Basically the sun was about to set, and the goal was that they reach Banu Qurayzah before Salat al-Maghrib.

So the Prophet made the commandment in the early day, and he said to them in the city of Madinah, "Make sure that you pray Asr in Banu Qurayzah." By the time they got ready, by the time they put their armor on, by the time they marched out of the city, it was already after Dhuhr; Maghrib was about to come. Maghrib came on the way to Banu Qurayzah. The Prophet ﷺ was already there waiting for them; he was at Banu Qurayzah. This is after the Battle of Khyber. Listen to the Seerah and you will understand this incident.

So the Sahabah differed, and essentially, this is the difference: should we follow the letter of the law or the spirit of the law? Should we literally pray Asr in Banu Qurayzah, which means let the sun set, let Maghrib come, let us not pray Asr, we walk and march, because we want to follow the Sunnah? And the other group says, no, no, we want to follow the Sunnah, and the Sunnah is that we expedite getting to Banu Qurayzah, but we still pray Asr over here.

My point is, neither of these two groups accused the other of not wanting to follow the Sunnah. Both of them wanted to follow the Sunnah, and our Prophet was silent at this, and he allowed both interpretations. He did not castigate, he did not rebuke one side over the other, because he knew that this was a legitimate attempt to derive the Sunnah. And the same applies in this issue over here.

So before I even began the fiqh of it, I wanted to discuss a little bit about the psychology and say, dear brothers and sisters, this is an issue like all the other issues. Let us remove the emotionalism and the instinctual reaction. No one wants to discard the Shari'ah, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah. Both of these groups want to see which of the positions is more in line with the goals of the Shari'ah, more in line with what Allah intended for the ummah, or even for a group amongst the ummah. And each of these sides, insha'Allah, is rewarded. Each of these sides wants to follow the Sunnah. Each of these sides is sincere.

So even if we choose one position, we should respect the other one and allow it, and not have any division within our hearts — that, no doubt about it, is what is haram. So even if one group gives zakat on jewelry and the other one doesn't, one group prays Jumu'ah before zawal and the other group doesn't, one group prays Asr before the other group's timing — so what? It's all within the acceptable spectrum, as long as we have reputable ulama who have shown us, hey, this is the legitimate position. And when it comes to this issue, there are plenty of ulama on both sides.

So we can agree to disagree. We can respect one position and not follow the other one. But what we should never do is divide our hearts. What we should never do is accuse the intention of the other side, to say that they don't want to follow the Sunnah. That is something that should not be done.

Now, that was the psychology of it. I have given a much longer lecture online about the fiqh issue; you will find it. I will summarize some of those points and add to them in today's lecture.

I want to mention that for most of Islamic history, for the bulk of Islamic history, the controversies that were raised about moonsighting were of a nature that didn't have to do with calculations. It was: how many witnesses must be seeing the new moon? How many witnesses? Where do they stand? Can they stand on the mountain or not, for example? Can they use a telescope or not? So you have in the early books of fiqh, and the books written for the first thousand years, a number of controversies in this regard. The issue of calculations was not a major issue for most of Islamic history, for multiple reasons.

And one does find references to the issue of calculations, and one finds that some ulama felt that in some circumstances, perhaps even in more circumstances, depending on which 'alim you followed, calculations could be utilized. And the primary reason why calculations were not seen in a positive light is the famous hadith, which is in Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, muttafaqun 'alayh, that our Prophet ﷺ said: "We are an ummi — we are an unlettered nation, a nation that is not educated, an illiterate nation." Ummi means you cannot read and write, right? Even in Urdu, ummi means you cannot read and write. "We are an ummi ummah. We don't write, nor do we calculate. The month consists of" — and then he motioned with his fingers — "29 or 30 days." The month consists of 29 or 30 days.

So when he said, "La naktubu wa la nahsub — we don't write and we don't calculate," from this many of the scholars then viewed the whole notion of calculation as being something that should not be done. Now, that has not been the only position, even from early Islam. There have been positions that are different to this one, and of them we're going to mention the great scholar of the Tabi'un, Mutarrif ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir, who died 95 Hijrah, and others as well. They considered that at certain times and situations, one can resort to calculations.

Now, on the other side, we actually have those ulama who went so far as to say that all types of calculations, even when it comes to the prayer timings and the prayer charts, should be avoided. And some ulama even took this hadith and extrapolated it to include any type of instrument, any type of thing that is used for the salah — so much so that one of the great scholars of this ummah, a great 'alim and a faqih and a muhaddith, and somebody we respect immensely (and when I quote these opinions, I'm not intending to denigrate; I'm simply demonstrating: if you want to take this hadith at face value, be consistent, and there are those who did, and we respect their consistency) — the great scholar Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali said that we don't use any type of calculations, even for our salah timings — what we call the prayer charts; we do the prayer charts. He said we should avoid this, and he said this is something that is a Jewish custom altogether.

And some of the ulama even said that we are not allowed to use a compass to figure out the direction of the Qiblah. This is something that is even reported from some of the senior scholars — maybe even Imam Ahmad himself, but definitely some of the senior scholars of the Hanbali madhhab. They said, because of this hadith, "Nahnu ummatun ummiyyah," we should not even use compasses to figure out the direction of the Qiblah. And so at least we will say that they were consistent in this regard.

Now, the majority of scholars, obviously, in our times use compasses and use prayer charts. So they have to take these things out of that hadith — and they do this — and they say, oh, but this is allowed and those are not allowed. One group of scholars said, hey, the hadith does not mean that we never use calculations. It is simply describing the status quo. It is describing the situation and not prescribing how things should be.

And amongst those is the great scholar Ibn Qutaybah — sorry — and Ibn Surayj, the Shafi'i scholar who died 306 Hijrah. Also, Ibn Rushd mentions this position as being a position that is known in the early Maliki school as well. Amongst those scholars as well is al-Khattabi from the Maliki school, 388 Hijrah; al-Qarafi, one of the greatest of the Maliki ulama, died 684 Hijrah; and al-Subki of the Shafi'i madhhab, who died 771 Hijrah.

Al-Subki, in his Fatawa, volume one, page 210, actually has a very, very long quotation in which he is arguing — this is 800 or 700 years ago. Al-Subki was one of the greatest ulama of the Shafi'i school, and he has written many books and treatises on theology, on fiqh and whatnot. And he has an entire section in his Fatawa, around two, three pages, where he discusses the issue of calculations. And he claims, in his time, 700 years ago, that the science of astronomy has now reached a level of yaqin, and that the visual sighting of the moon is not yaqini. Hence he said, now the Shari'ah will take the yaqin over the non-yaqin. This is what al-Subki is saying.

What is the summary of this? Al-Subki is saying it is very common for somebody to see something in the sky and think it is the moon. This is al-Subki writing 700 years ago. Can you imagine? Now we know this to be a fact; everybody thinks they've seen it. Al-Subki is saying people are uncertain whether it is the moon or not, they make a mistake, whether it is this, whether it is that, and calculations are certain. So he is arguing that in fact the Shari'ah would say, go with certainty over uncertainty.

And he also mentions that, as for those people who don't understand astronomy — this is al-Subki writing 700 years ago — as for those who don't understand how precise this science is... And al-Subki was an astronomer as well; he was somebody who understood the science of astronomy. Actually, he has some treatises — well, not separate treatises, but he's written about this in his writings.

And by the way, Muslims were at the forefront of astronomy. As you are aware, most of the stars of the skies are named in Arabic, and so many of the instruments were named and made by the Muslims. And the reason for this, by the way, was that they wanted to find the direction of the Qiblah — despite the fact that some small group of ulama always continued to maintain that the Qiblah should not be found via any type of calculation; rather, it should be done by other mechanisms.

Nonetheless, al-Subki argued that anybody who studies astronomy is aware of how certain that science is, and therefore they can appreciate that we should be going with calculations. And then he says, as for the one who doesn't know the science of astronomy, there's no point talking to this person, because they don't understand how certain the science is. He says, "Wal-jahilu la kalama ma'ahu" — we don't speak with somebody who doesn't know the science.

Now, if this is al-Subki writing 700 years ago, what do you think in our times, when the level has reached a different level of certainty? Again, anybody who studies the science of astronomy will tell you, look, we can calculate the birth of the new moon down to a millisecond. And if you doubt this, all you need to do is look at eclipses. Any time an eclipse happens, the local news agencies will tell you exactly when it begins and when it ends, and you can see for yourself, down to a millisecond.

Nobody can calculate when you can see the moon. However, we can calculate when the moon will be born. What's the difference between the two? When the moon will be born is an astronomical, mathematical, precise, physical calculation, and that is when the sliver of the moon will first catch the rays of the sun and be able to bring them back to earth — because, again, the moon obviously does not change in size; it is the rays of the sun that reflect back onto us. We can very easily calculate when the moon will be astronomically born. What we cannot calculate is when the person will see it.

Why? Because seeing the moon is dependent on many factors. Of them: how sharp is your eyesight? You cannot calculate that. Of them: the clarity of the atmosphere, whether there's some type of dust or particles or whatnot. Of them: are there shadows, or are there clouds in the sky or not? So all of these — atmospheric density, pressure — all of these things come into play. Whether you can see the moon or not, nobody can predict that. And it is possible that two people are standing next to each other, and one of them can see it and one of them does not see it. Or one of them thinks they're seeing it, and they're not seeing it.

Point being, all of this is to say that this notion of astronomical calculations being an unprecedented fiqh position is false. We have a number of ulama in the past who did argue for calculations. Now, was it a majority position? Never. But it existed.

In recent times, we have had a growing number of ulama argue that calculation should be given precedence in all circumstances. And this was the position of the greatest mujaddid of the last century, al-'Allamah Rashid Rida, who was the first — you can call him a global mufti — the first 'alim who, in our modern times, came to fame. He passed away in 1935, so 100 years ago from now. Rashid Rida is well known. Everybody knows Rashid Rida as one of the first global muftis, if you like. He's addressing modern challenges: the creation of the nation state, the collapse of the Ottoman Empire — all of these things happening in his time frame. A very learned, very forward-thinking, but also very traditional 'alim. Everybody knows him. Rashid Rida was of the first to write a treatise, a fatwa, arguing that for modern times we should adopt calculations as the default.

And this was followed by many ulama, including the Shaykh al-Azhar, the grand scholar of al-Azhar in the 1940s; his name is Muhammad Mustafa al-Maraghi. So the Shaykh al-Azhar, which is like the authority of al-Azhar, also wrote a treatise in this regard. As well, the great Salafi 'alim, the Ahl al-Hadith 'alim — so this isn't some progressive, modernist liberal — Ahmad Shakir is his name, who was the greatest 'alim of hadith in the 1950s. Before Shaykh al-Albani came, there was Ahmad Shakir. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir wrote many treatises of hadith; what he's most famous for is his critical editing of the Musnad of Imam Ahmad.

And Shaykh Ahmad Shakir, who only died maybe around 40 or 50 years ago, wrote a book on this issue. I have read this book, and I strongly encourage all the Arabic speakers to read it; you will find it online. He wrote an entire treatise on this issue, and again, he's arguing from a hadith perspective. I'll summarize some of his arguments in a while.

As well, some of the great ulama of the 80s and 90s: Shaykh Mahmud Shakir, the historian and the faqih and the 'alim; Shaykh Ali Tantawi — every Arab knows Shaykh Ali Tantawi — a Syrian person of letters, of noble birth, a very erudite, very well-read scholar; he passed away maybe 15–20 years ago. Shaykh Mustafa al-Zarqa, again a worldwide, global shaykh, a Syrian shaykh. Of course, Shaykh Yusuf al-Qaradawi is at the forefront of this as well, and he's still alive, in his 90s now — late 80s, early 90s. Shaykh Ali al-Qaradaghi, one of the leaders of the fiqh councils of the world; Shaykh Hassan al-Shafi'i in Egypt, a very learned scholar; Shaykh Abdullah al-Judai, again well known in England; Shaykh Faysal Mawlawi, who was one of the greatest scholars of Lebanon. He also argued for this issue of calculations.

Now, these people by and large were arguing for the entire globe — i.e. the Muslim lands and the Muslims in non-Muslim lands — to follow calculations. They're saying that we should change over to the default in this regard. Now, this was also the fatwa that was adopted by the European Fiqh Council and the Fiqh Council of North America, and many ulama, as I said, in this regard.

What did they say about the hadith? When the hadith says we are a nation that is ummi, we don't write and we don't calculate, what did they do with this hadith? Well, if you read their treatises and their fatawa, there are a number of things that they did. Just like, again, the hadith of giving zakat on gold, on jewelry: it's not that the hadith says it and khalas, there are no exceptions. Rather, the hadith is there, then you have other hadith as well, and you have other principles of fiqh that are brought in. The job of the faqih is not just to take a hadith and that's it, ignore everything else. The job of the faqih is to take the hadith as the source, and then see when we apply it, and when we apply other rulings based on other hadith.

And if you look at what these ulama said, they have a number of ways to resolve this issue. Of them is that the famous Shafi'i scholar Ibn Surayj, and also Ibn al-Shikhkhir, mentioned that, look, this hadith might be the default, but exceptions can be made. And of those exceptions, they argued that when it is cloudy, for example, we should go with calculations. Why should we leave it to uncertainty? When it is cloudy, we will go with calculations.

A number of ulama, including Rashid Rida, made a very profound point. He said the act of worship is the Salat al-Eid, not to see the moon — the Salat al-Eid, and also Ramadan, basically. To see the moon is not the actual act of worship; it is the means to the worship.

And the example that is given is the carpets that have the lines in them. Is it the goal of the Shari'ah that we look at each other before salah and try to straighten our lines? Or is it the goal of the Shari'ah to have straight lines? Because if the goal of the Shari'ah is to have straight lines, then we should have carpets that have lines in them — because the Prophet ﷺ did not have carpets with lines in them. The Prophet ﷺ himself would walk through the sufuf, and he would see the lines, and he would go after every saff and make sure everybody was correcting the line.

Now some ulama, even to this day — one of the famous muhaddithin of Syria, Jordan, originally from non-Arab lands, the famous muhaddith — would say that we should not have carpets with lines in them, and he says this goes against the Sunnah. Why? Because the Prophet ﷺ would walk through the lines and visually check them. So he said the goal of the Shari'ah is that the imam is walking through and physically checking the sufuf. That's his opinion; we respect him and his opinion. But the majority of ulama said no: walking through the sufuf is not the goal. The goal is straight lines. If we can achieve straight lines with carpets with lines in them, then why not have them?

And the same goes with this issue here: the goal of the Shari'ah is to begin and end the month. And when we now have the knowledge to begin and end the month in a manner that maybe previous nations or previous generations did not have, we can resort to that for the betterment of the ummah.

Also, another issue that one finds — and this is again beyond the scope of our lecture, because this is a very basic lecture here — is that if you read some of the earlier fatawa that are against calculations, it is quite clear that some of our early ulama — not all of them, some of them — conflated astrology and astronomy. Astrology is shirk and haram. Astrology is to think that looking at the stars will tell you your future. And astronomy is of course the physics, the science of the stars: what they are, naming them, their movements, etc., their categorization. This is a science, whereas astrology is mythology; it is nothing, no basis.

In some of the fatwas that we read from the past, it is very clear that they took all of this as one science, and they said that dabbling in the celestial spheres is going to lead to sihr, it's going to lead to black magic, it's going to lead to invoking the jinn. So they shut this door — this is some ulama. And of course that shows some of the reasons why they were hesitant to open this door.

Also, Shaykh Ahmad Shakir — one of the main things that I like about his treatise, and again I encourage all of you to read it. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir is coming from a Salafi paradigm, and I say this because some of our brethren think that this is a progressive opinion. No: some of the ulama that loved the Sunnah, that protected the Sunnah, also argued for this, and Ahmad Shakir is one of many of this nature. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir writes that this hadith — "We are an ummi ummah; we don't read, we don't write" — is not meant to prescribe a fiqh position. Rather, it is a description of the status quo. It's a description, not a prescription. This is what Ahmad Shakir argues.

And how does he argue this? Simple. Who amongst us goes back to the first part of the hadith and says we should remain illiterate, we should not learn how to read and write, we should not learn mathematics, we should not learn science, because the hadith says we are an ummi nation? So if you want to follow the next part of the hadith, follow the first part as well. This is the argument of Ahmad Shakir.

Ahmad Shakir is arguing: you have misunderstood this hadith completely. The Prophet is speaking to his time and place, and he is saying, given that we are an ummi ummah, given that we cannot read and write, let us keep things simple. He is not saying we should forever not read and write. We all know this: Iqra' is the first revelation, and the Battle of Badr incident of teaching the people how to read and write. He is not prescribing, until the Day of Judgment, that we should remain illiterate. None of us believe this. He is not prescribing that we should not learn mathematics.

The hadith literally says: we are an ummi nation; we don't read, we don't write, we don't calculate. Well, guess what? The entire ummah is reading and writing and calculating. So why do we cut off the first part of the hadith and make such a big issue about the last part? There seems to be some inconsistency. And Ahmad Shakir says the hadith has been misunderstood by the camp that thinks it is wrong to rely on calculations. That's a very interesting point that really does give food for thought.

Now, all of these are good positions. I actually, respectfully, have a different position, even though I lean towards calculation. My position is as follows. The position that I hold is that the statement for calculations is not the default. The previous ulama that I quoted — Ahmad Shakir and Rashid Rida and all of them — are arguing that calculation is the default and we should go with it. I'm not arguing that. I am saying that the default, in an ideal land — if we had power and sulta, and if we had tamkin; it's called an ideal land — we should follow the Sunnah of looking at the moon and going with the moon when we see it, because that is the Sunnah. There's no question, as the default.

However, what I'm arguing — and this is the argument of the European Council and others — is that, **given our current circumstances, the position of calculations becomes the shar'i position, and it is in conformity with the goals of the Sunnah, because of our context and not because of the text.**

Because you see — again, a bit of a technical issue here, and this is well known to all students of fiqh — sometimes there is a stronger position, which is called al-qawl al-rajih, and there is a weaker position, which is called al-qawl al-marjuh. Sometimes the weaker position becomes the stronger, not because of the textual evidence but because of the contextual situation. This is a very important point, and I want everybody to understand it. Now again, this is a rule that really nobody denies. Every student of knowledge, every faqih, every jurist accepts the rule. Of course, the devil is in the details, as they say. The question is: when is it applied? This is the issue.

What I'm arguing is the following — and this is the position of the Fiqh Council — oh sorry, not the Fiqh Council of North America; the European Fiqh Council. The Fiqh Council of North America is arguing like Shaykh Rashid Rida, which is that it is the default across the globe, and I'm not arguing for that. What I'm arguing is that the default in an ideal situation should be moonsighting: we see the moon. However, given the circumstances of us living in a minority land, and given the goals of the Shari'ah, it is better for us to follow al-qawl al-marjuh, the lesser-strength position, and it becomes the better opinion, and it becomes the rajih, because of the context and not because of the text.

Now, this rule is well known. Imam al-Subki says that if the mufti wants to follow the lesser opinion over the stronger one because of a benefit that goes back to the community, then this is permissible. This is al-Subki saying this. Al-Hafiz Ibn Rajab — who himself said we should not use calculations even for prayers, and some of his teachers and whatnot said don't even use the compass — Ibn Rajab says that whoever understands these issues of fiqh knows that a lot of times, in certain societies, especially in later times, we should follow the less strong position over the stronger opinion because of the time that we live in, because of the zaman that we are in. This is al-Hafiz Ibn Rajab saying this.

Ibn Taymiyyah also points to this. Again, I'm quoting these ulama to tell you the rule. I'm not saying they said calculations — no. I'm saying Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn Rajab, all of them are arguing that sometimes the lesser position becomes the stronger one because of the context. Ibn Taymiyyah says in Majmu' al-Fatawa, volume 24, page 198, that sometimes the marjuh, the lesser position, becomes the rajih, the stronger one, because of the benefit it brings the ummah. This is the argument that I myself and many of my teachers and the people that I look up to are making.

Al-Shatibi, one of the greatest scholars of usul al-fiqh and one of the greatest authors on the goals of the Shari'ah, says that when the mufti gives the fatwa, he doesn't just look at the texts; he looks at the consequences of the fatwa. And he says that the fatwa is never looked at in isolation from its reality. You never look at a fatwa from a theoretical perspective; you look at a fatwa from a contextual perspective, and then you make the judgment call.

So, given the context, and given how we have seen ourselves... And again, I will be the first to say: 25 years ago, when this issue first came to light in North America, I was of those who were also opposed to the notion of calculations. And year by year, decade by decade, we see the negatives of this position, we see the cons, and we see the pros of the other position. And so slowly but surely, being in the community, seeing the national and international and local debacle and the drama and everything happening, you come to realize that the context that we are in dictates that we follow the lesser position, which is not as strong ideally, but which is going to make the ummah better.

And this is not a position of liberalism or progressive Islam. It is a position for which we have a basis. Al-Subki argued for it. Rashid Rida argued for it. Ahmad Shakir argued for it. Many European... even the Council of Turkey — there was a symposium seven, eight years ago about the Islamic calendar, where ulama from across the globe came, and they also adopted, and they also petitioned to have, calculations as well. This isn't a position that is coming from far left field. That's what I want to stress upon you. It's not coming from those same groups that want to legitimize immoralities and fahisha. This is coming from mainstream ulama whom we respect and we love, and they are looking at the situation and saying, for the time and place that we live in, this position seems to make more sense.

And they are saying the hadith is valid; indeed the Prophet did say, "We are an ummi nation." But firstly, maybe the hadith is not meant to be applied universally. And secondly, even if one believes that the ideal interpretation is that we shouldn't do calculations, perhaps in our context it becomes the better of the two.

Now again, who's going to decide? It is the ulama. So what I suggest the average Muslim do, or the boards of their communities do, is to choose which 'alim or which group of ulama they're going to follow. That's your choice. And then after that, go with either of the two opinions, and don't look down on or create division in your heart against the other position.

Now the question arises: why am I arguing that, and why are the groups that I look up to arguing that? There are many pros to the calculation position. What are the pros of the calculation position? What are the pros of the moonsighting position? As for the main pro of the moonsighting position, the main argument that they use is: we're following the Sunnah. And that's great, and we respect and we admire them for that. Alhamdulillah, may Allah bless you, may Allah reward you. Their main point is, this is the Sunnah and we want to stick with it.

I humbly point out that fiqh is not taken from a literal hadith. Just like I gave the example of the zakat on gold jewelry: the majority of the ummah did not take the literal wordings of the hadith, and I can give you many more examples. Every student of knowledge is well aware: you don't just find the hadith and then derive fiqh. Hadith are the data points; hadith are the general sources that we use. It's the source, but there's something called usul al-fiqh. There's an extraction process, and that extraction process is where fiqh is actually done.

So understand that just because the hadith says it doesn't mean it needs to be applied in every single circumstance. The job of the faqih is not the job of the muhaddith. The muhaddith tells you whether the hadith is authentic or not. The faqih says: what are the exceptions? Where do we apply it? Where do we not apply it?

And again I go back to the hadith of Banu Qurayzah. The Prophet ﷺ said one thing — "Pray Asr in Banu Qurayzah" — in his own lifetime, and the Sahabah split into two camps. Because how do you understand it? In what circumstances? What if something else happens? Should we ignore it? Should we not ignore it? All of these things are where usul al-fiqh comes into play. I am not claiming that calculation is the right answer. I am saying calculation is the better answer, given the circumstances we are in.

What are some of the pros of calculations? Well, where does one begin? There are so many masalih, they're called — so many pros that one has. First and foremost, everybody is aware of the bitter disputes that happen in the masajid, amongst the people, within the community: the last night of Sha'ban, the last night of Ramadan, the late phone calls, the drama, the back and forth, the animosity about whether you're going to accept this moonsighting or that moonsighting, the politicization even. Again, I'm sorry to be blunt here, but certain countries' moonsighting is not accepted by other countries because of politics, right?

So all of this — the chaos, the drama — will be eliminated. And wallahi, this is one of the main goals of the Shari'ah: to eliminate bickering, eliminate the animosity. If you know in advance, we're going to follow the position of ISNA, the position of the Fiqh Council — khalas. These last-minute phone calls and the bickering will be eliminated. This is one of the goals of the Shari'ah.

As well, we now have the possibility of a larger group of Muslim unity, or at least unity within one locality. We are already aware that within North America, as the latest survey shows, the majority of masajid — I think when they did the survey, I think over 60–70% of the masajid within North America... I'm not talking about within one community per se; obviously within North America there are pockets that follow here and there. But as a whole, of the many thousands of masajid in North America, most of them are now following the position of the Fiqh Council and ISNA, which is calculation.

So we now have a large group. I'm living in the Dallas area, for those of you watching this from other cities — even in the Dallas area we've had masajid following calculation since the 80s. So it's not as if it is unprecedented. We have masajid that are following this, and slowly but surely, more and more are gravitating towards this position.

As well, we can achieve family harmony. Because, subhanAllah, how many times is a father praying in one masjid and a son praying in another masjid, and now they're split up because of this issue? We can try to achieve a larger sense of unity in this regard.

Also, by following calculations, what happens is that we now know exactly when Eid is going to be and when Ramadan is going to be, so we avoid wasting the money and the resources of the community. When I was in Houston, I remember clearly there were times when the masjid would have to book the main hall or the grand convention center for two days — pay double the fees — because we didn't know which day Eid was going to be. Saving the money of the ummah is definitely of the goals of the Shari'ah.

And of course, perhaps the biggest issue here is: what is the goal of Eid? It is to gather the people together. That is the primary goal of Eid. As for looking at the moon, is it a direct goal or not? Scholars have differed: is it a goal, or is it a means to the goal? Again, back to the issue of the sufuf and the lines: what is the goal? Is the goal looking at the moon, or is the moon the stepping stone to the goal? If the moon is the stepping stone to the goal, well, then calculations can take its place.

And you know what? Feel free to look at the moon for Sunnah. Go and look at the moon for 'ibadah, for 'ibrah, for seeing the beauty of Allah 'azza wa jall — as Allah says in the Qur'an, to look at the creation of Allah — but let the community have unity by following the calculations.

And what's going to happen here as well is that when you know when Eid is and when Ramadan is, the average Muslim, who might not even be that religious, will be able to take the day off for Eid. There are so many Muslims — may Allah guide us and them — who are not that practicing, and if Eid is unknown and it's not on a day that they're able to take off, they're not going to pray Eid.

And the main goal of Salat al-Eid — the Prophet literally said, and the hadith is in Bukhari — let everybody come, even women who cannot pray. Can you imagine? Women who are in the monthly cycle — the Prophet said, let them come to the Eid salah so they can see the barakah, see the khayr. This is one of the goals of the Shari'ah: to have a massive Eid salah. Even if you're not praying, for a legitimate excuse, you should come.

This is the goal of Eid, not to look at the moon. That's secondary. That's good if you're able to do it, but if you're not able to do it, then to have a larger congregation is a bigger goal. And let's be honest here: if everybody knows when Eid is, months in advance, then insha'Allah ta'ala everybody with an ounce of iman is going to take that day off. Everybody who has any issue is going to say, "You know what, insha'Allah I'm going to take Thursday off. I'm going to tell my boss. I'm going to reschedule my exam, this and that, tell my teacher, my professor, whatever. I'm going to take that day off."

That is the goal of the Shari'ah, far above going outside and seeing the moon. That is good, that is Sunnah, that is an act of worship, insofar as looking at the skies is an act of worship. But the argument that I'm making is that the ultimate goal is the congregation of the ummah.

And of course, we also have to think as a minority here. New York and New Jersey, for example — New Jersey is close by — New York has already declared Eid to be a federal holiday. I'm speaking to you from Texas. Texas and California are the next states in terms of Muslim population. We have the potential to declare Eid to be a holiday for our children. Now how is that going to happen if we don't know when Eid is going to fall? How is that going to happen?

So again, if you want to have this notion of preserving Islam for the next few generations... So many of us pray regularly — may Allah bless all of you and keep us amongst them — and so many of us don't realize that the majority of the ummah does not pray five times a day. For every one person who comes to the masjid, 10, 15, 20 hardly ever come. All you need to do is look at Eid in those communities that have one Eid. I remember in Houston we would get 30, 40,000 people sometimes for Eid, and we wondered: where are these people for Jumu'ah? Where are these people for the daily salawat? There are people for whom that's their only attachment with Islam.

Their children — and I have met people like this — in their adulthood have come back to Islam; they've become religious. I have met numerous people who have told me, "In the 80s and 90s, the only time our parents took us to a mosque or to a Muslim gathering was on the day of Eid." I have met people like this. They are there, and they represent that critical area: if we don't cater to them, if we don't reach out to them, it is very possible that the next generation will simply lose their iman.

I am arguing that calculations will help for that segment. I'm not going to say it's going to save 100%, but it will help. It will make them remember that "we went to Eid with our parents." They know when Eid is going to come, and they're going to be able to pray over there.

And also, dear brothers and sisters, as somebody who's been active in the North American scene for 25 years — I mean, of course I'm born and raised here, but even in terms of preaching and teaching, actually more than that; my first khutbah was given pretty much 30 years ago — so as somebody who has seen, from the late 80s, early 90s, as an active Muslim in the da'wah scene, I will tell you that more and more imams, more and more religious clerics, more and more students of knowledge are sympathetic to calculations.

However, what they're worried about is community backlash. I have spoken to numerous imams across this country who have told me, "I wish we could go with calculations, but I'm worried that my community will reject it." And I said to them, "Who is the scholar of your community — you or your community?"

Why is this such an emotional issue, where you want to just backlash and say this is haram or bid'ah or not allowed, when so many reputable ulama... Dear Muslims, I don't want to be so blunt here, but every one of us is following fatawa that are a bit of a compromise: when it comes to health insurance, when it comes to credit cards, when it comes to living in the situation we're living in. We're taking concession after concession after concession. And there's nothing wrong with that, because the Shari'ah does not want to place a burden that is unreasonable on us. No 'alim in a theoretical utopia would allow a credit card. Almost every one of us has a credit card. We're using technology in so many areas of our lives, and we're using it for religious issues as well. Yet for this one issue we say, oh, it is haram, or the hadith is against it.

And I understand some ulama interpreted the hadith to mean it is against it. But I just explained to you, even in this there are two opinions, and many ulama said no, the hadith is not against it; it is an interpretation that is against it. But in reality, nobody follows the first part of the hadith. Nobody says, let us remain uneducated because the Prophet ﷺ said we are an uneducated ummah. No, he is not telling you to remain uneducated. He is simply describing the situation and saying, given the time that we live in, let's keep things simple and keep fasting when we see the moon.

So my argument is very simple, dear brothers and sisters, and that is that the position of following calculations is better in the long run: for our own survival, for our children, for our communities, for our congregations, for the quantity of people that come, to save our resources, to plan things out. The masalih, the pros — check, check, check, check, check — keep on going.

On the other side, what is the main pro? The thought that they are following the Sunnah, which is, alhamdulillah, a great intention; we ask Allah to reward them. But essentially that's the only pro. As for the cons, keep on going: the bickering and the animosity and the breaking away and the tempers and the uncertainty, and you keep on going. And once you start following this other position, that is pretty much eliminated.

So when you look at it: the main goal of the Shari'ah is Muslim unity. The main goal of the Shari'ah is maximizing Eid attendance. The main goal of the Shari'ah is facilitating the people to have their rituals. And if you follow this other position, which is the position of so many ulama, then all of this will be met. And therefore, I argue, the lesser position, the marjuh, becomes the rajih. It becomes the goal of the Shari'ah, given the circumstances that we are in.

Nonetheless, after all is said and done, this is an opinion. It is the position I have very passionately argued, but this passion does not at all mean that the other position is wrong. On the contrary, I respect the other position. Whoever sincerely wishes to follow whichever position, alhamdulillah. Let our hearts remain united even if you want to follow the other position. And I say this in all honesty, dear brothers and sisters: listen, if you are very certain that your position is the better one, no problem, follow it. But don't create controversy within your community, and whatever you do, do not break your hearts away from other Muslims who follow the other position.

SubhanAllah, we follow different positions in so many areas, and yet our hearts remain united. Did you ever have a fight with somebody who pays zakat on jewelry, if you don't pay zakat, or with somebody who doesn't? And this hadith, by the way, says if you don't pay zakat you're going to Jahannam, or the fire of Jahannam is on you. Did you have a fight over this issue? No. So then why will you fight over an issue that is not even anywhere near as explicit as the other hadith are? This is indeed a gray area. We've had major ulama on both sides of this issue.

I strongly feel that one of the reasons why we are so emotional is that we have misunderstood this fatwa to be a very progressive or very liberal fatwa, and we feel that it has no basis in Islamic fiqh. And that is frankly incorrect. It does have a basis in Islamic fiqh. It has precedents. It has early authorities, it has authorities in medieval and middle Islam, and it has modern authorities. It is not unprecedented. And in our times it is becoming more and more popular, and great ulama are adopting it. If you wish to follow it, alhamdulillah — and I feel it is better for the North American context. And if you wish not to follow it, alhamdulillah.

And I want to give a message especially to our own community here in the Dallas area: these two positions are both practiced in the greater Dallas area. There have been masajid for the last 20 years following this position and following that position. If your local masjid is following a particular position, my general advice is to follow their position, no problem. If you are that adamant that you disagree with your local masjid, whatever that masjid might be, then no problem: go to the other masjid and pray with them, and don't make any type of breaking away of ranks or hearts, because our hearts are one, despite the fiqh position. No problem; agree to disagree with respect. More important than any fiqh position is unity.

And by the way, last year the American Muslim Jurist Association and the Fiqh Council of North America — they are on polar opposite sides when it comes to this issue. The American Muslim Jurist Association argues for global sighting; the Fiqh Council, which I'm a member of, argues for calculations. They both released a joint statement that both of these positions are valid, but we prefer X, we prefer Y; follow your community and do not create a scene or break ranks or break hearts. Both bodies have different positions, and they said unity is more important.

Both of them said follow your local masjid, whatever your masjid says. Even AMJA, which does not agree with calculations from a fiqh perspective, said if your masjid follows calculations, follow calculations. And the Fiqh Council, and I'm a part of it, says the same thing: if your masjid says moonsighting, follow your masjid. No big deal. There should not be this level of animosity that has happened.

I want to conclude by quoting a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ and an incident from Ibn Mas'ud (radiallahu 'anhu). As for the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, he mentioned in the famous hadith in Tirmidhi — the Prophet ﷺ said that the day of the fast is the day that you all fast, and the day of Eid is the day that you celebrate Eid. This hadith is in Tirmidhi. What does this mean? The Prophet ﷺ is saying, whatever day you guys do it, that's going to be the day. Don't worry about what's happening up there, what's happening in the skies, whether it's the moon or not; don't worry.

"As-sawmu yawma tasumun, wal-Eid yawma tuftirun." The day of fasting is the day that all of you have come together to fast, and the day of Eid is the day that you all celebrate Eid. This is a hadith in Tirmidhi. And this shows us that what is more important is what your community is doing. Even if a community is mistaken or whatnot, to stick with the community is better.

And that's why I want to conclude on this issue with the famous incident of Ibn Mas'ud and Uthman. Ibn Mas'ud had a certain position about praying Dhuhr and Asr in Mina during the days of Hajj: that it should be done as two raka'ah and should not be done as four raka'ah. And he gave the fatwa; he said everybody should pray two raka'ah for Dhuhr and Asr at Mina. And Uthman (radiallahu 'anhu) had the opinion that Dhuhr and Asr should be prayed as four raka'ah in Mina. So he led the salah and he prayed four raka'ah. When Ibn Mas'ud saw this and heard this, he prayed four raka'ah behind Uthman (radiallahu 'anhu).

The students of Ibn Mas'ud said, "O Shaykh, didn't you just give us the fatwa earlier today that we're supposed to pray two raka'ah? Yet here you are praying four raka'ah behind Uthman." Ibn Mas'ud said, "Yes, I did say that two raka'ah is the Sunnah to pray, but breaking away from the jama'ah is a worse sin than praying four raka'ah behind the imam here." In other words: I'm weighing the pros and cons here, and my position is it should be two raka'ah, but breaking away from the jama'ah and finding your own jama'ah is a worse issue than, in my opinion, praying four raka'ah of Dhuhr and Asr in Mina. This is what you call the fiqh of the Sahabah. This is real knowledge, dear brothers and sisters.

And I want to tell you a personal anecdote. The masjid I was in before this, for reasons beyond the scope of this, followed a position that I did not personally agree with, but I stuck with them because of the unity of the city. In the city I was in, all of the masajid — they came to me and they said, if you want, we can break away and follow the position that you want. And I said no, because the city is united. In that city, I said no, we're not going to break away.

However, given that in other cities there is no unity — we have masajid here and there — and it is very clear that the tide is shifting towards the other position, I think that it is the wiser thing for those that are able to do so — it's up to the boards, it's up to the imams — for those that are able to do so, for the future of the ummah.

Nonetheless, when all is said and done, dear brothers and sisters, this is an opinion. It is a position, and Allah 'azza wa jall alone knows what is ultimately the truth. We are striving, we are trying, we are doing what we think is best, and we have to answer to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. **And my advice to all of you is to follow your local masjid, whatever the position is.** If they go with global, go with global. If they go with local moonsighting, go with local moonsighting. And if they go with calculations, go with calculations. Stick with your masjid. It's not a major issue at the end of the day.

And if you are on the board, and if you have to make the decision, that is when you need to do some research and ask around. If you are following and you're just going to the masjid, stick with your masjid, and don't create any issues with somebody that might have another opinion. At the end of the day, our unity is more important than whichever fiqh position we follow. We ask Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to always guide us to the truth, and always make us of those who see the truth and act upon it.
